newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr learns to live with rate anxiety.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr learns to live with rate anxiety.

text.p: The Australian dollar held its nerve Friday and rallied from key support as yet another rate cut scare proved wide of the mark.
The currency looked close to breaching the crucial US$0.7910 level after weak wages and inflation data this week whipped up rumours the Reserve Bank would ease as early as this morning.

In the event the RBA remained mum, allowing dollar bulls to breathe easier for another day. "It was hairy for a while there this morning, but exporters were keen to buy the dips when it became clear the RAB wasn't easing," said one. "The odds still favour a cut, but the market's fed up of worrying about it."
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar had bounced to US$0.7938/43 from an early US$0.7920/25 and US$0.7915/20 late here Thursday.

Resistance was seen at US$0.7945 and, more importantly, the month high of US$0.7985. If US$0.7910 were to crack, dealers expected stop loss selling to drag the currency to US$0.7880 and put at risk the important US$0.7850 level which marks lows both this month and last.

The currency also recouped losses on the crosses to hit 89.73/83 yen and 1.2081/96 marks from 89.25/35 and 1.2014/40 late Thursday. In trade weighted terms it nudged up to 58.7 from 58.6, which was not far from Monday's five year high of 59.1.
The local unit was aided on the crosses by a slide in the yen which saw the U.S. dollar clear the important 113.00 yen barrier after days of effort.

Dealers said Japanese investors continued to pour funds offshore as interest rates there looked set to remain at record lows for months yet. he Australian dollar, with its relatively high yields, was one of the major beneficiaries of this exodus and such was the premium that even the heightened threat of an easing by the RBA had hardly deterred the Japanese demand.
Thus the futures market had priced in a 0.5 point cut, but the AUD was only just short of a four year high on the yen.

Traders thought the currency was still likely to come under knee-jerk pressure if the RBA were to cut rates, but doubted it would turn into a rout given that any cut was expected to be the last in the easing cycle.
Current betting is that the RBA will move after its next monthly board meeting on November 5, but analysts emphasised it would not be a surprise if it eased on any morning next week.

The only data out were September motor vehicle registrations which showed a 0.2 percent gain to 54,290. This was a firmer result than appearances would suggest since analysts had expected a small fall and it followed a hefty 7.0 percent rise.
The figures, which are notoriously volatile, would have no bearing on the chance of a rate cut but still suggested the consumer was not as weak as bears and the soft employment data, would imply.
Analysts also noted that quarterly retail sales data next week were sure to show consumption made a big positive contribution to GDP growth in Q3.
Along with strong net exports and inventories, it should see GDP growth of around 0.6 percent up from 0.2 percent in Q2 which would produce not unrespectable annual growth of around 3.1 percent.

Also due next week are current account data for September which should show another tolerable deficit of around A$1.3 billion, and building approvals for September which are expected to be flat after a couplde of months of healthy gains.
